summary: Psalm 45 presents itself as a wedding song for the king. It first praises the king’s beauty, speech, military power, just rule, and richly adorned court, then turns to the daughter who is entering the royal household. The closing verses look beyond the ceremony to royal descendants and a remembered name among the peoples.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows the Psalter’s royal and ceremonial voice, where poetry, music, courtly honor, and hopes for lasting rule meet. Later readers have often heard more than a historical wedding here, but the chapter itself first depicts a king, a bride, and the public hope attached to their house.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with the sons of Korah; Psalms headings can mark authorship, association, collection, performance, or dedication, and their exact historical force is debated.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; individual poems may come from the monarchy through the postexilic period, so one precise date for Psalm 45 cannot be established from this chapter alone.
context.setting: A royal wedding setting is named in the heading, with imagery of the king, queen, palace, gifts, garments, music, and future princes.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry within the Psalter; specifically a royal wedding song with a heading, praise, address, and blessing.

outline.heading: The poet begins
outline.note: The heading names musical and performance associations, and the speaker introduces a noble theme for the king.

outline.heading: The king addressed
outline.note: The poem praises the king’s beauty, gracious speech, splendor, majesty, victory, and power over enemies.

outline.heading: The throne and royal court
outline.note: The king’s rule is described with equity, righteousness, anointing, fragrant garments, music, ivory palaces, honorable women, and the queen in gold.

outline.heading: The daughter addressed
outline.note: The poem tells the daughter to turn from her former household toward the king, and imagines gifts and favor coming to her.

outline.heading: The procession
outline.note: The princess appears in gold and embroidered work, accompanied by virgins, and enters the king’s palace with gladness.

outline.heading: A remembered name
outline.note: The final blessing looks to sons who become princes and to the king’s name being remembered by all generations.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. Set to “The Lilies.” A contemplation by the sons of Korah. A wedding song. My heart overflows with a noble theme. I recite my verses for the king. My tongue is like the pen of a skillful writer.
keyVerses.why: The opening tells readers what kind of poem this is: a performed wedding song offered for the king.

keyVerses.text: Your throne, God, is forever and ever. A scepter of equity is the scepter of your kingdom.
keyVerses.why: This is the chapter’s strongest statement about throne, kingdom, and just rule, and it has been especially important in later interpretation.

keyVerses.text: Listen, daughter, consider, and turn your ear. Forget your own people, and also your father’s house.
keyVerses.why: The poem shifts here from addressing the king to addressing the woman entering the royal household.

keyVerses.text: I will make your name to be remembered in all generations. Therefore the peoples shall give you thanks forever and ever.
keyVerses.why: The closing expands the wedding scene into a hope for lasting remembrance and public gratitude.

questions.question: What kind of psalm is this?
questions.answer: The first verse calls it “A wedding song,” and the rest of the chapter fits that setting. It praises a king, addresses a daughter who is entering the king’s household, describes rich garments and a palace procession, and ends with hopes for royal descendants and lasting remembrance.

questions.question: Who are the sons of Korah?
questions.answer: The chapter’s heading says the poem is “by the sons of Korah.” Psalms is a many-voiced anthology, and headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging, so the phrase should be treated as real evidence without forcing one exact modern meaning.

questions.question: Why does the poem speak so strongly about the king’s beauty and power?
questions.answer: The chapter is formal praise for a royal wedding, so it uses heightened court language. The king is called excellent, blessed, mighty, splendid, majestic, victorious, and armed against enemies. That language presents the king as an ideal ruler in the poem’s ceremonial moment.

questions.question: Does verse 6 call the king God?
questions.answer: Verse 6 says, “Your throne, God, is forever and ever,” and verse 7 immediately says, “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you.” Readers differ over how to understand this royal language in its first setting and in later reception. Some read it as exalted address connected to the king’s throne and office; Christian readers have often read it messianically, especially because the verse is connected with Christ in later interpretation, but that later use should not erase the psalm’s royal wedding setting.

questions.question: What does “anointed” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: The word appears in the line, “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows.” In the chapter, it marks the king as honored and set apart with joy. The verse also connects his anointing with his love of righteousness and hatred of wickedness.

questions.question: Why are myrrh, aloes, cassia, ivory, and gold mentioned?
questions.answer: These details create a picture of royal abundance and ceremonial beauty. The king’s garments are fragrant, music comes from ivory palaces, and the queen stands in gold of Ophir. The poem does not pause to explain each item; it uses them together to make the wedding scene feel costly, public, and splendid.

questions.question: Why is the daughter told to forget her people and her father’s house?
questions.answer: The poem addresses the daughter as someone entering the king’s household. In the scene, she is told to listen, consider, turn her ear, and leave her former household behind. The wording reflects the social movement of the wedding scene; it should not be lifted out of that ancient royal setting as a direct rule for all marriages.

questions.question: Who is the daughter of Tyre?
questions.answer: Verse 12 says, “The daughter of Tyre comes with a gift.” In the chapter, this figure belongs to the public honor surrounding the royal wedding, where wealthy people seek favor. The chapter does not identify a specific historical individual, so it is best to read the phrase as part of the poem’s scene of royal tribute and prestige.

questions.question: What happens at the end of the poem?
questions.answer: The focus moves from the wedding procession to the future of the royal house. Sons will take the place of fathers, become princes, and the king’s name will be remembered in all generations. The last line imagines the peoples giving thanks forever and ever.

A royal staff used here as an image of the king’s rule; the chapter says the scepter of his kingdom is one of equity.
A place name linked here with gold; the queen is pictured standing at the king’s right hand in gold of Ophir.
One of the fragrances named on the king’s garments, contributing to the royal wedding imagery.
